title: Delay of infrastructure works in a lot development
summary: The buyer sued over late infrastructure works and asked for presumed lost profits, a contractual penalty and moral damages. The judgment found the developer in delay for sixteen months and granted lost profits only; the developer's pending appeal attacks the percentage alone.

pages: EXCELENTÍSSIMO SENHOR DOUTOR JUIZ DE DIREITO DA 2ª VARA CÍVEL DO FORO DE CIDADE EXEMPLO – UF

SICRANA DE TAL, brasileira, professora, portadora do CPF nº 000.000.000-00, residente na Rua Imaginária, 300, Cidade Exemplo – UF, por seu advogado (Dr. Beltrano Advogado, OAB/ZZ 000.000), vem, respeitosamente, à presença de Vossa Excelência propor a presente
AÇÃO DE INDENIZAÇÃO POR ATRASO NA ENTREGA DE OBRAS DE INFRAESTRUTURA C/C DANOS MORAIS
em face de LOTEADORA EXEMPLO S.A., CNPJ nº 00.000.000/0001-00, com sede na Avenida Modelo, 200, Cidade Exemplo – UF, pelos fatos e fundamentos a seguir.
I – DOS FATOS

Em 20 de maio de 2094, a Autora adquiriu da Ré o lote 7 da quadra B do Loteamento Parque Modelo, pelo preço de R$ 80.000,00 (oitenta mil reais), integralmente quitado. A cláusula 6.1 do contrato fixa o prazo previsto para conclusão das obras de infraestrutura: 24 meses, contados da assinatura, prorrogável conforme cronograma aprovado pela Prefeitura. As obras deveriam, portanto, estar concluídas em 20 de maio de 2096.

As obras de pavimentação, drenagem e rede elétrica somente foram concluídas em 30 de setembro de 2097, com a emissão do Termo de Verificação de Obras pela Prefeitura, ou seja, com dezesseis meses de atraso. Durante esse período a Autora, que pretendia construir sua residência no lote, ficou privada do uso do bem.
A cláusula 6.3 do contrato estabelece multa de 1% (um por cento) ao mês sobre o valor do contrato em caso de atraso no pagamento das parcelas.
II – DO DIREITO

A mora da Ré é evidente e decorre do simples decurso do prazo contratual. Nos termos da jurisprudência consolidada, o atraso na entrega do imóvel gera direito a lucros cessantes presumidos, correspondentes a 0,5% do valor do contrato por mês de atraso, independentemente de prova do prejuízo. Aplica-se o Código de Defesa do Consumidor.
A multa da cláusula 6.3 deve ser aplicada em favor da Autora, por equidade, já que o contrato só prevê penalidade contra o consumidor.
A privação do uso do lote por mais de um ano, com a frustração do projeto de construir a casa própria, configura dano moral indenizável.
III – DOS PEDIDOS

Ante o exposto, requer: a) a declaração da mora da Ré a partir de 20 de maio de 2096; b) a condenação da Ré ao pagamento de lucros cessantes de 0,5% do valor do contrato por mês de atraso, de 20 de maio de 2096 a 30 de setembro de 2097, no total de R$ 6.400,00 (seis mil e quatrocentos reais); c) a condenação da Ré ao pagamento da multa contratual de 1% ao mês prevista na cláusula 6.3, invertida em favor da consumidora, no total de R$ 12.800,00; d) a condenação da Ré ao pagamento de indenização por danos morais no valor de R$ 15.000,00 (quinze mil reais); e) a condenação da Ré nas custas e honorários.
Dá-se à causa o valor de R$ 34.200,00.
Cidade Exemplo, 10 de fevereiro de 2098.
Beltrano Advogado – OAB/ZZ 000.000
EXCELENTÍSSIMO SENHOR DOUTOR JUIZ DE DIREITO DA 2ª VARA CÍVEL DO FORO DE CIDADE EXEMPLO – UF

LOTEADORA EXEMPLO S.A., já qualificada, por seus advogados (Dra. Ciclana Defensora, OAB/ZZ 000.001), nos autos da ação que lhe move SICRANA DE TAL, vem apresentar CONTESTAÇÃO, pelas razões que passa a expor.
I – DO PRAZO CONTRATUAL

A cláusula 6.1 não fixa data certa: estabelece prazo previsto de 24 meses, prorrogável conforme cronograma aprovado pela Prefeitura. O cronograma de obras de um loteamento depende de aprovações e vistorias do Poder Público, de modo que o prazo é estimativo. Não há mora automática pelo simples decurso de 24 meses.
II – DA FORÇA MAIOR

Entre janeiro e agosto de 2096, a região registrou chuvas muito acima da média histórica, conforme laudo meteorológico anexo (doc. 2), o que paralisou as obras de terraplenagem e drenagem por meses. Trata-se de força maior (art. 393 do Código Civil), que afasta a responsabilidade da Ré pelo atraso.
III – DA CONCLUSÃO DAS OBRAS
As obras foram concluídas e verificadas pela Prefeitura em 30 de setembro de 2097, conforme o Termo de Verificação de Obras (doc. 3). O loteamento está integralmente entregue.
IV – DOS LUCROS CESSANTES E DA MULTA

A Autora não comprovou qualquer prejuízo. A presunção de lucros cessantes é inaplicável e, de todo modo, o percentual de 0,5% é excessivo. A multa da cláusula 6.3 é devida apenas em caso de atraso no pagamento das parcelas e não pode ser invertida contra a Ré.
V – DOS DANOS MORAIS
O atraso de obras, por si só, não gera dano moral. A Autora limita-se a alegar frustração, sem demonstrar abalo concreto. A jurisprudência é pacífica nesse sentido.
VI – DOS PEDIDOS
Requer a improcedência dos pedidos. Junta o contrato (doc. 1), o laudo meteorológico (doc. 2) e o Termo de Verificação de Obras (doc. 3).
Cidade Exemplo, 15 de abril de 2098.
Ciclana Defensora – OAB/ZZ 000.001
SENTENÇA
Vistos.

SICRANA DE TAL ajuizou ação de indenização em face de LOTEADORA EXEMPLO S.A., alegando atraso de dezesseis meses na conclusão das obras de infraestrutura do lote 7 da quadra B do Loteamento Parque Modelo. Pede a declaração da mora, lucros cessantes de 0,5% ao mês (R$ 6.400,00), a multa da cláusula 6.3 invertida em seu favor (R$ 12.800,00) e danos morais de R$ 15.000,00.

A Ré contestou, sustentando que o prazo da cláusula 6.1 é estimativo, que houve força maior por chuvas atípicas, que as obras foram concluídas com Termo de Verificação de Obras e que não há prejuízo, multa invertida ou dano moral.
É o relatório. Decido.

O prazo da cláusula 6.1, ainda que prorrogável conforme cronograma aprovado pela Prefeitura, tem termo certo de 24 meses, e a Ré não demonstrou qualquer prorrogação formalmente aprovada. A mora está configurada a partir de 20 de maio de 2096.

A alegação de força maior não prospera: o laudo meteorológico juntado é genérico e não demonstra nexo entre as chuvas e a paralisação das obras, tampouco o período exato da paralisação. Chuvas são fato previsível na atividade de loteamento.

Reconhecida a mora, são devidos lucros cessantes presumidos, correspondentes a 0,5% do valor do contrato por mês de atraso, de 20 de maio de 2096 a 30 de setembro de 2097, dezesseis meses, no total de R$ 6.400,00. Anoto que não há nos autos prova de que a Autora tenha requerido alvará de construção ou agendado visita técnica ao lote, mas a presunção de prejuízo dispensa tal prova.

A multa da cláusula 6.3 é improcedente: a cláusula prevê penalidade apenas para o atraso no pagamento das parcelas, e sua inversão em favor da consumidora, na ausência de previsão contratual, não pode ser imposta pelo juízo.
Os danos morais são improcedentes: o atraso na conclusão de obras de infraestrutura, sem outras circunstâncias, não ultrapassa o mero aborrecimento.
DISPOSITIVO

Ante o exposto, JULGO PARCIALMENTE PROCEDENTE a ação para: (i) declarar a mora da Ré a partir de 20 de maio de 2096; (ii) condenar a Ré ao pagamento de lucros cessantes no total de R$ 6.400,00 (seis mil e quatrocentos reais), corrigidos monetariamente desde cada mês de atraso e acrescidos de juros de mora de 1% ao mês desde a citação; (iii) julgar improcedentes os pedidos de multa contratual e de indenização por danos morais.
Sucumbência recíproca: custas rateadas e honorários de 10% sobre o valor da condenação em favor do patrono da Autora e de 10% sobre o valor dos pedidos improcedentes em favor do patrono da Ré.
P.R.I.
Cidade Exemplo, 5 de novembro de 2098.
Sicrana Julgadora – Juíza de Direito
EGRÉGIO TRIBUNAL DE JUSTIÇA DO ESTADO – UF
Apelação Cível – Processo nº 0005678-42.2099.8.26.0002
Apelante: LOTEADORA EXEMPLO S.A. – Apelada: SICRANA DE TAL
RAZÕES DE APELAÇÃO
I – DA TEMPESTIVIDADE E DO PREPARO
O recurso é tempestivo e o preparo foi recolhido, conforme guia anexa.
II – DAS RAZÕES PARA A REFORMA

A r. sentença merece reforma quanto ao percentual dos lucros cessantes. O percentual de 0,5% ao mês sobre o valor do contrato é excessivo para um lote sem edificação, que não gera renda de aluguel. A jurisprudência admite percentuais de 0,25% em casos de lote, devendo a condenação ser reduzida para R$ 3.200,00.
III – DO PEDIDO
Requer o conhecimento e o provimento do recurso para reduzir os lucros cessantes a 0,25% do valor do contrato por mês de atraso, com a redistribuição dos ônus da sucumbência.
Cidade Exemplo, 2 de dezembro de 2098.
Ciclana Defensora – OAB/ZZ 000.001

map:
1. IDENTIFICATION OF THE CASE
Parties: SICRANA DE TAL (plaintiff, buyer of lot 7, block B, Parque Modelo) v. LOTEADORA EXEMPLO S.A. (defendant, developer, the client). Stage: judgment of 5 November 2098; the developer's appeal, filed 2 December 2098, is pending. Contract: purchase of a lot dated 20 May 2094, price R$ 80.000,00, fully paid; clause 6.1 sets an expected term of 24 months for the infrastructure works, extendable according to the schedule approved by the municipality; clause 6.3 provides a penalty of 1% per month for late payment of instalments. Amount in dispute: R$ 34.200,00.

2. THE PLAINTIFF'S CLAIMS
- Declaration of the developer's delay from 20 May 2096.
- Presumed lost profits of 0.5% of the contract price per month of delay, sixteen months, R$ 6.400,00.
- The penalty of clause 6.3 (1% per month) reversed in the consumer's favour, R$ 12.800,00.
- Moral damages of R$ 15.000,00 for the frustrated plan to build a home.
- Costs and fees.
Grounds: automatic delay on the expiry of the contractual term; case law presuming lost profits on late delivery; CDC; equity for the reversal of the penalty.

3. THE DEFENCE, PLEADING BY PLEADING
Defence (contestação): clause 6.1 is an estimated term extendable according to the municipal schedule, so there is no automatic delay; force majeure from unusually heavy rains between January and August 2096 (weather report, doc. 2); the works were completed and verified by the municipality on 30 September 2097 (certificate of completion, doc. 3); no proof of loss, the 0.5% presumption is inapplicable and excessive; clause 6.3 applies only to late instalments and cannot be reversed; no moral damages for a delay of works. Documents: the contract, the weather report and the certificate of completion.
Appeal (razões de apelação): attacks only the percentage of lost profits, arguing 0.5% is excessive for a bare lot that yields no rent and asking for 0.25% (R$ 3.200,00). Does not attack the starting date of the delay, the rejection of force majeure or the presumption of loss itself.

4. DEFENSIVE GAPS IDENTIFIED
- The estimated nature of the schedule (clause 6.1, extendable according to the municipal schedule) was pleaded but not proven: no approved extension was filed, and the appeal dropped the point.
- The judgment itself recorded that the buyer never requested a building permit or a site visit, yet the defence never used the buyer's inertia against the presumed lost profits or to argue a duty to mitigate.
- The force majeure finding (a generic weather report with no causal link) was not attacked on appeal.
- The presumption of lost profits for a bare lot was attacked on the percentage only, not on whether a lot yields rent at all.

5. EVIDENCE
Plaintiff: the contract, proof of full payment. Defendant: the contract (doc. 1), a generic weather report (doc. 2), the certificate of completion of 30 September 2097 (doc. 3). Missing: the municipal approvals and the extended schedule, site logs of the rain stoppage, evidence that the buyer never sought a permit or a visit.

6. DECISIONS
Judgment of 5 November 2098: the term of clause 6.1 is 24 months and no approved extension was shown, so the delay runs from 20 May 2096; force majeure rejected because the weather report is generic and shows no causal link with the stoppage; lost profits of 0.5% per month for sixteen months (R$ 6.400,00), noting that the buyer never requested a building permit or a site visit but that the presumption dispenses with such proof; the reversed penalty dismissed because clause 6.3 covers late instalments only; moral damages dismissed as mere annoyance; reciprocal costs and fees of 10%.
ULTRA PETITA: none (the award of R$ 6.400,00 equals the request).
FEES: no appellate decision yet.

7. LEGAL REGIME OF THE CONTRACT
A lot development under Lei 6.766/79, though no party cited the statute; the CDC was applied as the main regime. No fiduciary lien is mentioned. Force majeure was pleaded and rejected; no contributory fault or tolerance period was discussed.

8. SUMMARY TABLE
CLAIMS - FINAL OUTCOME:
- Declaration of delay from 20 May 2096 -> GRANTED - no approved extension of the 24-month term was shown
- Lost profits of 0.5% per month (R$ 6.400,00) -> GRANTED - presumed loss on late delivery; appeal pending on the percentage
- Contractual penalty of clause 6.3 reversed in the buyer's favour (R$ 12.800,00) -> DISMISSED - the clause covers late instalments only
- Moral damages of R$ 15.000,00 -> DISMISSED - a delay of works alone is mere annoyance
ULTRA PETITA: none
FEES INCREASED: not increased
DEFENCE WINS:
- contractual penalty -> DISMISSED - clause 6.3 provides no penalty in the buyer's favour
- moral damages -> DISMISSED - a delay of works alone does not cause moral damage
SPECIAL LAWS ARGUED:
- None - CDC and Civil Code only
ABSENT TOPICS:
- property tax
- fiduciary lien
- association fees
- rescission of the contract

complexity.rationale: Cumulative claims (delay, lost profits, a reversed penalty, moral damages) and one pending appeal. The matter is partly settled (presumed lost profits on late delivery) and partly controversial (whether the presumption fits a bare lot). The amount in dispute is low (R$ 34.200,00), the evidence is documentary and there are two parties.

risk.coverage: The defence answered every claim, but the answer on the term was an assertion without the approved schedule behind it, and the buyer's inertia recorded by the judge was never turned into an argument.
risk.evidence: The weather report was generic and the court said so; no site log, no municipal approval and no extended schedule were filed, so the estimated-term argument had nothing to stand on.
risk.appealStage: The pending appeal attacks the percentage of lost profits only. It leaves the starting date of the delay, the rejection of force majeure and the presumption of loss itself untouched, so a partial win at best.
risk.causation: The link between the delay and a loss was accepted tacitly: the defence denied the loss but never argued that a buyer who sought no permit and no visit lost nothing from the delay.
risk.summary: Medium risk: the exposure is small and two claims were dismissed, but the appeal is narrow and the strongest arguments on the term and on the buyer's inertia were left out.

theses.title: The estimated nature of the works schedule (clause 6.1) was not used to move the starting date of the delay, and the appeal dropped it
theses.anchor: prorrogável conforme cronograma aprovado pela Prefeitura
theses.analysis: Clause 6.1 makes the 24-month term extendable according to the municipal schedule. The defence said so but filed no approved extension, and the judgment fixed the delay at 20 May 2096 for that reason. The appeal did not attack the starting date at all, so sixteen months of delay are now settled.

theses.title: The buyer's inertia (no permit, no site visit) was never used against the presumed lost profits
theses.anchor: não há nos autos prova de que a Autora tenha requerido alvará de construção ou agendado visita técnica ao lote
theses.analysis: The judge recorded that the buyer never requested a building permit or scheduled a visit to the lot. A buyer who did nothing to use the lot suffered no loss of use from the delay, and the duty to mitigate points the same way. The defence denied the loss generically and never made this argument.

theses.title: The rejection of force majeure was not attacked on appeal
theses.anchor: o laudo meteorológico juntado é genérico e não demonstra nexo entre as chuvas e a paralisação das obras
theses.analysis: The judgment rejected force majeure because the weather report was generic and showed no causal link with the stoppage. The appeal did not challenge that finding or offer the site logs that would have shown the months of paralysis. The point is lost unless raised now.

theses.title: The 48-month regulatory term of Lei 6.766/79 as a possible thesis on the delay of works
theses.anchor: prazo previsto para conclusão das obras de infraestrutura: 24 meses
theses.analysis: The contract calls the 24 months an expected term. Lei 6.766/79 gives the developer a regulatory term to complete the infrastructure of a registered development, which supports the argument that the contractual term is an estimate and that delay is not automatic. Nobody cited the statute; it is a new argument for the appeal.

theses.title: The presumption of lost profits was attacked on the percentage only, not on whether a bare lot yields rent
theses.anchor: lucros cessantes presumidos, correspondentes a 0,5% do valor do contrato por mês de atraso
theses.analysis: The judgment applied a rental presumption built for finished homes to a bare lot. The appeal accepted the presumption and asked only for 0.25%. The prior question, whether a lot without a building yields any rent to presume, was never put to the court.

theses.title: Moral damages: the defence relied on generic case law
theses.anchor: O atraso de obras, por si só, não gera dano moral
theses.analysis: The defence denied moral damages with a general statement and no precedent on point. A specific line of decisions on delays in lot developments would have made the denial stronger.

theses.title: The property tax (IPTU) borne during the delay was not offset against the award
theses.anchor: Termo de Verificação de Obras pela Prefeitura
theses.analysis: The buyer paid property tax on the lot throughout the delay. The defence could have argued that the tax paid is a cost of ownership that offsets the presumed loss of use.

theses.title: Clause 6.5 caps the compensation at 5% of the price and was never invoked
theses.anchor: cláusula 6.5 – limitação da indenização a 5% do preço
theses.analysis: The contract caps the developer's liability for delay at 5% of the price in clause 6.5. The defence did not invoke the cap, and the award exceeds it.

theses.title: The defence did not answer the plaintiff's reliance on Lei 4.591/64 for the delivery deadline
theses.anchor: prazo previsto para conclusão das obras de infraestrutura
theses.analysis: The plaintiff argued that Lei 4.591/64 makes the delivery deadline binding, and the defence said nothing about the statute. The silence let the court treat the term as a hard deadline.

opportunities.title: Prove the estimated schedule with the municipal approvals, not with an assertion
opportunities.originInCase: Clause 6.1 pleaded as an estimated term without any approved extension filed (defence, page 2; judgment, page 3).
opportunities.suggestedPattern:
In every delay claim of the development, the defence must file the municipal approvals, the inspection reports and the extended schedule that clause 6.1 refers to. The argument that the term is an estimate is true only when the extension exists on paper; without it, every court will read 24 months as a hard deadline, as this one did.

The file for each phase of the works should be assembled once by the engineering team and reused across cases: approvals, inspection dates, stoppage orders, weather stoppages with site logs. A defence that shows the sequence of public acts moves the starting date of the delay or removes it altogether.

On appeal, the starting date of the delay is a ground on its own; an appeal that concedes it and argues only the percentage has given away most of the case.
checklist: Obtain from engineering the approvals, inspections and extended schedule for the phase of the lot
File them with the defence as the proof behind clause 6.1
Where the stoppage was weather, file the site logs with dates, not a regional report
On appeal, attack the starting date of the delay before the percentage

opportunities.title: Use the buyer's inertia against presumed lost profits in every lot case
opportunities.originInCase: The judge noted that the buyer never requested a permit or a site visit (judgment, page 3), and the defence never argued it.
opportunities.suggestedPattern:
Presumed lost profits were built for finished homes that could be rented. For a bare lot, the loss of use depends on what the buyer would have done with it. When the buyer never sought a building permit, never approved a project and never visited the lot, the defence must say so with the municipal records and argue both the absence of a loss and the duty to mitigate.

The argument also supports the prior question, whether a lot yields rent at all, and gives the court a reason to lower the percentage even where it keeps the presumption.

Ask the municipality for a certificate that no permit was requested for the lot; it is cheap and decisive.
checklist: Request from the municipality a certificate of permit requests for the lot
Check the visit log of the development for the buyer's name
Argue the absence of a loss of use and the duty to mitigate in the defence
Raise the prior question of whether a bare lot yields rent before discussing the percentage

opportunities.title: Appeal on every adverse ground, not only on the amount
opportunities.originInCase: The appeal asks for 0.25% instead of 0.5% and leaves the delay, the force majeure finding and the presumption untouched (appeal, page 4).
opportunities.suggestedPattern:
An appeal limited to the percentage concedes the delay, the rejection of force majeure and the presumption of loss. Each of those is an autonomous ground with its own chance, and an appellate court can only decide what is brought to it.

Draft the appeal from the judgment's reasoning backwards: for each adverse finding, state the ground, the evidence and the law. Keep the amount as the last, subsidiary ground, so a partial win on any earlier ground reduces or removes the award.

Where new evidence is needed (site logs, municipal certificates), consider whether the case allows it on appeal and, if not, use it in the next similar case from the start.
checklist: List every adverse finding of the judgment before drafting the appeal
Raise the starting date of the delay and the force majeure finding as separate grounds
Put the percentage last, as a subsidiary ground
Record which evidence was missing so the next defence files it from the start

planted.title: Moral damages: the defence relied on generic case law
The property tax (IPTU) borne during the delay was not offset against the award
Clause 6.5 caps the compensation at 5% of the price and was never invoked
The defence did not answer the plaintiff's reliance on Lei 4.591/64 for the delivery deadline
